entry.title: Gary Stevenson's inequality documentary: capitalism indicted, but is a wealth tax enough?
entry.summary: As an indictment of British capitalism the documentary is excellent. The trouble starts with the remedy: £24 billion is roughly one week of government spending.

entry.title: The Chinese revolutions of 1927 and 1949
entry.summary: A leadoff written for a CWI summer school. Two revolutions, one question: at each stage, what would you have done as a Marxist standing there, with the information available at the time?

entry.title: The 1926 general strike: working-class power on display
entry.summary: A leadoff written for the centenary of the general strike. For nine days the country stopped, the strike was solid and growing, and that is the moment its own leaders surrendered. Why, and what follows from it.

entry.title: Gaza, Lebanon and the anti-war movement
entry.summary: Nine pieces written for the Socialist across two and a half years of the war, from the first mass demonstrations in London to the assault on Lebanon. Collected here in reverse order.

entry.title: Marxist economics: the state of the world economy
entry.summary: A leadoff on the world economy. Everything that caused 2008 is still there, and four things have been added since: two major wars, a US-China trade war, protectionism, and sixteen years of low investment.

entry.title: Trump's war on the climate
entry.summary: Rescinding the endangerment finding would strip the legal basis from US climate regulation. Behind it lies a tactical shift, not a break with what the Democrats did before.

entry.title: China: state intervention, world economic crisis and class struggle
entry.summary: An introduction to the discussion on China at Socialism 2025. A Bonapartist state that bred its own capitalist class, and what happens to it when the growth that held the arrangement together runs out.

entry.title: Deadly and avoidable Hong Kong fire provokes widespread anger
entry.summary: At least 146 dead, a renovation site inspected repeatedly, alarms that never went off, and thirteen arrests within days. The comparison being drawn is with Grenfell, and the anger is running into a legislature nobody can stand for.

entry.title: China's revolutionary tragedy
entry.summary: Why, despite the courage and determination of the masses, the revolution in China that began one hundred years ago ended in defeat.

entry.title: Kenya: anger erupts again in a new wave of anti-government protests
entry.summary: Thirty-one killed in a single day, protests across seventeen counties, and an IMF bailout at the root of it. A movement that has bypassed the political parties entirely, and the question of what it turns into next.

entry.title: Councils, cuts and the fight for funding
entry.summary: Two pieces on local government, two years apart. A Croydon meeting on a 15% council tax rise, and a Unite protest outside parliament with a busload of Birmingham bin workers on it. The demand in both is the same: set a no-cuts budget.

entry.title: Starmer, Sunak and the case for a new party
entry.summary: Four pieces across two governments and one general election, on the King's Speech, the climate question on the doorstep, Starmer's first winter in office, and whether 800 Green councillors have made any difference.

entry.title: Capitalist climate hypocrisy: who should pay for the crisis?
entry.summary: Guyana's president asks the BBC a fair question. If the West values the forest, is it willing to pay for it? The answer exposes what a market cannot do.

entry.title: Defeating imperialist intervention
entry.summary: A review of Anna Reid's A Nasty Little War. Meticulously researched, politically bereft: it cannot explain why 180,000 imperialist troops lost.

entry.title: Bills, rents and who pays for the crisis
entry.summary: Four pieces from the worst of the cost-of-living crisis, on rent gouging, sewage in the rivers, free school meals and the biggest strike wave in thirty years. The same question runs through all of them.

entry.title: Students, young workers and the party
entry.summary: Four reports from stalls, demonstrations and a conference. Trafalgar Square after Roe v Wade fell, a £15-an-hour campaign in Seven Sisters, the Socialist Students conference in Birmingham, and a Chilean donor in Stockwell.

entry.title: Why I joined the Socialist Party
entry.summary: Written for the paper's regular column. What convinced me was not a meeting but a demonstration, and then finding out why the meetings discuss theory at all.

entry.title: A prophetic vision of the past
entry.summary: Written for AN404, Theory and Ethnography. The ethnographic present froze whole societies outside history so they could be salvaged. It can be reclaimed, but only by giving up the idea that anthropology is in the business of representation.

entry.title: Every view is a view from somewhere
entry.summary: Written for AN404, Theory and Ethnography. Anthropology's claim to objectivity rested on a distance between the knower and the known. Taking that distance apart is not a literary problem but a political one.

entry.title: Indigenous sovereignty and the resource assemblage
entry.summary: Written for AN479, Anthropology of Law. Sovereignty claims that look like a fight against the state often turn out to be a way of making land legible to capital, winning symbolic recognition while the political economy stays exactly where it was.

entry.title: Law is governance, imposed
entry.summary: Written for AN479, Anthropology of Law. If law is bound up with self-conscious projects of government, then calling every normative order a legal order loses sight of what makes law law, and of what it does when it arrives.

entry.title: Why the study of households matters for an analysis of the economy
entry.summary: Written for AN456, Anthropology of Economy. The household is presented as a natural unit standing outside the economy. It is neither natural nor outside, and is presented as such to allow for capital accumulation.

entry.title: Voter ID and the right to vote
entry.summary: Two pieces on the photo ID law, written either side of its first use in the May 2023 local elections. Three convictions for voter impersonation in seven years, and two million people without the right documents.

entry.title: The US must do more to combat carbon inequality in the global economy
entry.summary: Winning entry in the LSE Phelan US Centre climate change essay competition. National emissions accounts are the wrong unit: responsibility sits with the corporations and investors who own the emissions, and most of them are American.

entry.title: The economy is natural
entry.summary: Written for AN456, Anthropology of Economy. The presentation of a capitalist world economy as natural is a discursive tool for holding the everyday political order of capitalism in place, and anthropology is well placed to take it apart.
